meaning: (1) the son of Baldwin, from the nick. Bald, popularly Ball; (2) 'the bald'; (3) 'at the Ball,' a sign-name
author_comment: This was popularly Ball. The large number of Balls in the London Directory is accounted for by the great favour in which the name was held, and the constant influx from the Low Countries, where for a time it ruled supreme. The d in some cases might be dropped later on, on account of its suggesting baldness. We find Balcock in the Hundred Rolls, -cock being the suffix usually appended to the nick. of fontal names (v. Balcock). (2) v. Ballard. The representatives of this sobriquet have also dropped the final d to hide the truth. From either (1) or (2) or both came a pet name given to various animals. Ball is mentioned as the name of a horse in Chaucer and Tusser, of a sheep in the Promptorium, and of a dog in the Privy Purse Expenses of Henry VIII (Halliwell). 'Balle, schepys name': Prompt. Parv. p. 22. (3) cf. Bell, Roebuck, &c. This sign-name has existed for centuries.
source: Hundred Rolls, 1273
record_text: Custance Balde, co. Camb., 1273. A.
